steps.title: Without History, Edits Collide
say: Contoso's weather team ships a promotions API, and the team shares one promotions file.
Copies pile up, and one edit quietly overwrites another.
There's no history and no safe way to work in parallel. The team needs a shared history and a better way to work together.

steps.title: Version Control Remembers Every Change
say: Version control records what changed, who changed it, when, and why.
Because every change is remembered, any earlier version can be recovered.
And it makes parallel work possible, through branches.

steps.title: Git Is the Tool, GitHub Is the Platform
say: People mix these two up, so let's separate them. Git is a distributed version control tool that runs on your computer.
GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration on top. Git is open source and works fine without GitHub.
Push, pull, and clone move commits between your computer and GitHub.

steps.title: Repository, Commit, Branch
say: Three ideas to know. A repository holds your files and the history of each one.
A commit is a snapshot in time, saved with a message. Every real commit has an author, a time, and a message.
A branch is a separate line of work, kept apart from main until you're ready.

steps.title: Accounts: You, Your Team, Your Company
say: You sign in to a personal account, with GitHub Free or GitHub Pro.
Organizations bring teams together, with shared accounts, teams, and roles.
Enterprise accounts manage many organizations, with central policy and billing. Plans change, so check GitHub's plans page.

steps.title: GitHub Flow: Six Simple Moves
say: GitHub flow is a lightweight, branch-based workflow. You work on a branch, ask for review, merge, then tidy up.
First you branch and commit, which keeps your work safely away from the default branch.
Then a pull request asks for feedback, and a merge lands the changes on main. You can do each move on the website, the command line, or in GitHub Desktop.

steps.title: Review, Merge, Done
say: Here's the flow in action. Maya opens a pull request from her branch.
Ravi reviews it and approves the changes. Then the pull request is merged, and the branch gets deleted.
Deleting the branch is safe. The pull request and its commits stay, and the branch can be restored.

steps.title: Markdown Makes Issues and PRs Clear
say: Markdown turns plain-text symbols into headings, lists, task lists, and code.
An at sign mentions a person and notifies them. A hash and a number links to an issue or pull request.
It works in issue and pull request descriptions, in comments, and in README files.

steps.title: Pick the Tool That Fits the Moment
say: It's the same repository, but with different doors: the website, GitHub Desktop, GitHub Mobile, an editor, or the command line.
GitHub Desktop is a free, open source app for Windows and macOS, with visual Git and no commands to memorize.
GitHub Mobile, for Android and iOS, brings notifications, reviews, and comments to your phone.

steps.title: Git and GitHub Basics, All in One
say: Let's recap. Version control keeps the history, Git is the tool, and GitHub is where the team works together.
You've covered repositories, commits, branches, accounts, GitHub flow, Markdown, and picking the right tool.
